newsitem.title: UK: IRA suspect shot dead in British raid was unarmed.
newsitem.headline: IRA suspect shot dead in British raid was unarmed.

text.p: British authorities acknowledged on Wednesday that an IRA suspect shot dead in a dawn raid was apparently unarmed, but police defended their action.
Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army, accused British police of killing an unarmed man when they seized arms and explosives during raids in London on Monday.
Police said they believed that Diarmuid O'Neill, who died in a hail of bullets, was armed and a dangerous guerrilla. They had only a split second to react when bursting in to a London guesthouse.
Five other people were arrested and 10 tonnes of explosives seized in raids that dealt a severe blow to the guerrilla group battling to oust Britain from Northern Ireland.
Defending police tactics after a search revealed no weapons in O'Neill's room, one senior police officer said: "This man had to be regarded as a very, very dangerous individual."
"We believe him to be a terrorist and our knowledge of terrorists, especially those in the IRA, tells us that they are often armed and willing to kill," he told the Daily Mail.

Newspapers said detectives had firmly linked O'Neill with a bomb factory found in a London warehouse and believed he was leader or quartermaster for an IRA cell on the point of launching bombings and assassination attempts in Britain.

Sinn Fein, political wing of the IRA, said "no exchange of fire took place" when O'Neill died. An inquest into O'Neill's death opened on Wednesday and a London coroner allowed O'Neill's body to be released to his family for burial.

The police complaints authority, which is investigating the shooting, said it was far early to say what happened. Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, said the case should not be pre-judged.
The European Court of Human rights condemned Britain after plainclothes commandos shot dead three unarmed guerrillas in 1988 in the British colony of Gibraltar.
Media profiles of O'Neill painted a picture of a model pupil seduced by the Republican cause.
He was said to idolise IRA hunger striker Bobby Sands and sold Republican newspapers in London pubs as a teenager.
He worked as a clerk for the Bank of Ireland in London but was charged with embezzling money siphoned off for the Republican cause. He was sentenced to one year's youth custody in 1988.
The dawn raids quashed speculation that the IRA planned an imminent renewal of their 17-month ceasefire, shattered in February with a bomb in London that killed two people.
Mayhew, speaking to British and Irish parliamentarians, echoed growing pessisism about the chance of Sinn Fein joining all-party talks that have become bogged down in wrangling.
"Let me say that the evidence of the IRA's preparations for more attacks is a massive contrast with their talk of peace," he said.
